paper_title: Answering in the User's Variety: Calibrated Accommodation Pairs for Post-Training

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: People adapt how they talk to the person in front of them. However, chat models tend to respond in Standard English regardless of the dialect used by the user. A uniform answer can hide whether training treats these users alike, and output audits cannot tell as well. We trace how each post-training stage, from supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to preference optimization (DPO) and reinforcement learning, changes a model's tendency to match the user, and read what each update prefers from two content-matched replies, one matching the user and one not. Across 10 open model lineages, post-training standardizes replies to every informal cue, yet after adjusting for how likely each reply already was, the DPO update still favours matching British and Australian spelling over AAE and Singlish on 10 lineages, and models still produce AAE features when asked. We then introduce calibrated accommodation pairs (CAP), preference data that reward matching users' dialect density while preserving Standard English for Standard-English users. On a fully open model, CAP raises convergence on features it was not trained on without a detectable increase in dialect for Standard-English users or a cost in instruction following. In contrast, one-sided pairs reach a similar gain only by overshooting the user and imposing dialect. Our findings show that uniform replies can hide selective updates and audits should read the update as well as the output. Code: https://github.com/kouzhizhuo/cap-accommodation.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: A user asks chatbot for advice: usually buy theater tickets for my sister, who keep dragging me to the movies. My boss says the budget been canceled this month. Do yall have any tips? (Figure 1; replies in Section C.1.1) The request is in African American English (AAE); its StandardEnglish twin differs only in keeps, has been and you. People adjust their speech to the person they Figure 1: Standard replies vs. selective updates. Top: Post-training uniformly reduces outputs across all English varieties. Bottom: While replies across all varieties converge on Standard English, preference tuning specifically favors matching British spelling over stigmatized varieties. talk to, converging toward that persons way of speaking or holding back (Giles et al., 1991), and deployed chatbots over-converge to their users style (Blevins, 2026). Yet chat models default to Standard English with speakers of AAE, Singlish and Nigerian English (Fleisig et al., 2024). Features of these varieties are rare in chatbot traffic and training data (Section C.2). Instruction-tuned models converge less to dialogue style than pretrained ones (Blevins et al., 2026), reward models disprefer AAE (Mire et al., 2025), and dialect gaps accumulate along the training pipeline (Elle, 2026). Two questions remain open. First, closed models and base-versus-instruct comparisons cannot tell which stage installs this default: supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on standard responses, or preference optimization. Second, outputs alone cannot tell whether training treats users alike: two models that answer everyone in Standard English may have learned different preferences. We read accommodation on two channels at every training stage: the reply (does it converge toward the users variety?) and the update (does the training step favour converging?). We follow 10 open lineages through SFT, direct preference optimization (DPO) and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR); each checkpoint answers requests like the one above, written in several varieties and in Standard English. We score only reply text not copied from the request, and read each update through the likelihood it gives to two content-matched replies, one that matches the user (your sister, who keep dragging you) and one that does not (who keeps dragging you). Our contributions are as follows: ❶ Standard replies, selective updates. Post-training defaults to Standard English, but DPO selectively favors British and Australian spelling over AAE and Singlish on all 10 lineages. ❷ Controlled rerun. Accommodation-consistent pairs boost convergence only at high doses, while undesirably introducing dialect for Standard English users. ❸ Calibrated accommodation pairs. Penalizing under-accommodation, over-accommodation, and imposition in DPO data increases held-out convergence on OLMo-2-1B without dialect insertion. ❹ Diagnostic & benchmark. We introduce copycontrolled convergence ratio and matching bonus to disentangle output behavior from training preferences (anonymous code and data). Several pre-registered predictions did not hold, including that the split between prestige and stigmatized varieties grows at the preference stage, and that convergence rises gradually with the dose of accommodation-consistent preference pairs; Section D.2 reports every outcome. Whether model should reply in users variety is for its speakers to decide (Sandoval et al., 2025).

sections.title: 2 Background and Related Works
sections.content: Accommodation. Communication Accommodation Theory (CAT) holds that speakers adjust their speech to interlocutors for social reasons (Giles et al., 1991; Giles, 2016). Convergence reduces linguistic differences to seek approval, divergence accentuates them, and maintenance keeps ones own variety; convergence flows upward, toward the higher-status variety, and speaker able to converge may choose not to (Dragojevic et al., 2016). Priming accounts instead predict convergence to every variety (Pickering and Garrod, 2004), as in pretrained model continuing users turn. Language models converge strongly when completing human dialogues, instruction-tuned ones less (Blevins et al., 2026); these studies measure style, we measure the features that distinguish varieties.1 language ideology. StandardStandard language ideology treats one variety as correct and the others as errors (Milroy, 2001; Lippi-Green, 2012). It predicts upward convergence toward the standard and prestige cues such as British spelling, but not toward stigmatized grammar. Language models show covert prejudice against AAE speakers (Hofmann et al., 2024), reward models disprefer AAE (Mire et al., 2025), preference tuning creates dialect disparities (Ryan et al., 2024), and generative AI is argued to reproduce the ideology (Smith et al., 2026); we ask where in training it enters. Reading training update. DPO makes the logratio between the trained and the reference policy an implicit reward (Rafailov et al., 2023). We use the ratio between consecutive released stages descriptively, as an update diagnostic, not an identified reward: compared across content-matched replies, it shows which reply stage upor downweights. We pre-registered predictions from these accounts before the main runs (Section D.1); related work is in Section E.1.

sections.title: 4 Replies Converge on Standard English
sections.content: As Figure 3 shows that post-training makes replies standard for every user, while the ability to produce dialect features remains. 4.1 Post-Training Standardizes Replies to Every Informal Cue Post-training standardizes replies to every informal cue ( Table 1). Base OLMo-2-7B reproduces users British spelling at 0.171 (95% CI [0.137, 0.207]); after SFT the rate is 0.120, after DPO 0.058 ([0.040, 0.076]), and RLVR leaves it at 0.060. Informal register follows the same path (0.413 at base under the chat template, 0.009 after DPO). The preference stage, with the chat template fixed, lowers convergence to informal register on all 10 lineages and to British spelling on 9 of 10 (stage and framing details in Section C.4). The exception is formal register. Replies keep converging to formal requests at every stage (OLMo-2-7B after DPO: 0.141), so post-training not replies formal. Dialect grammar was mirrored only weakly to begin with. Continuing users text, base OLMo-2-7B reproduces AAE features at 0.022 ([0.013, 0.031]) and Singlish lexis at 0.051. After SFT both are near zero, also on human-written AAE tweets (Section C.1). The ordering by prestige is already present in the base model. Convergence follows the preregistered prestige tiers at base (ρ = 0.778 on OLMo-2-7B) and after DPO (ρ = 0.845): posttraining lowers the level of convergence but does not install the order. The decline holds at scale and across popular families (Table 2 and Figure 4). From base to final release, informal-register convergence falls in all 12 further families, Britishspelling convergence in 9, and AAE ends at most 0.001. Deployed chatbots standardize AAE too, but partly answer Nigerian Pidgin in kind: across 5, convergence is at most 0.053 for informal register and 0.009 for AAE, while British spelling is reproduced at 0.0890.207 and Nigerian Pidgin at 0.1160.502, above any post-trained open model (at most 0.046; Table 6). In open models, post-training standardizes replies for users of every variety, not singling out stigmatized varieties. 4.2 Models Still Produce AAE Features on Request Two of three families still produce AAE features at more than half their authentic rate when asked (Table 12 in Section C.1). Asked to reply in the users variety, OLMo-2-7B after DPO realizes AAE features at 0.567 of their authentic rate, against 0.009 in its default replies; Tülu-3-8B behaves alike (0.588). OLMo-3-7B reaches 0.411; rates are corrected by the blind human audit (Section C.4). Requested imitation increases stereotyping (Fleisig et al., 2024), so competence measures ability, not reply quality. AAE features are produced on request in all three families, at more than half their authentic rate in two rarely by default.

sections.title: 7 Discussion
sections.content: Output audits find one Standard-English answer for every user; the update diagnostic, read from public checkpoints without retraining, shows training moving the policy toward matching some users and away from others. Model releases should report it next to output audits. The standard default arises with little dialect-specific data (under 1% of preference prompts) and is not inevitable, since deployed chatbots answer Nigerian Pidgin in kind. The prestige ordering in the update is consistent with prestige-directed convergence but does not identify prestige as its cause, and raw and adjusted contrasts answer different questions, so update diagnostics should report both (Section C.3).

sections.title: 8 Conclusion
sections.content: Along every released stage of open model lineages, post-training standardizes replies to every informal cue, prestige spelling included, while the training update favours matching prestige spelling over stigmatized varieties, and models still produce AAE features on request; adding accommodationconsistent pairs to third of the DPO data raises held-out convergence over matched controls in every run, though without calibrating it. Calibrated accommodation pairs address that failure: on OLMo-2-1B they raise held-out convergence with no detectable increase in dialect for StandardEnglish users, though explicit requests for Standard English still receive some, whereas one-sided pairs built the same way reach similar gain only by overshooting the users density and imposing it. Uniform replies can hide selective update; audits should read the update as well as the output.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: We study English, six varieties and open lineages up to 32B whose every stage is public; closed chatbots enter only through their behaviour. All requests are rule-based renderings that are not calibrated to the feature densities of authentic text, so convergence on real users writing may differ; only competence and check on human-written AAE twins (Section C.1) are anchored in authentic text. Our detectors cover finite feature inventory, and human validation rests on consensus labels for sample of 84 items, which the part-of-speech formality score failed and the GYAFC-trained ranker passed; the CAP and WildChat checks are consensus labels on samples too, with no independent double annotation, so inter-annotator agreement is not reported. The update diagnostic describes what each stage favours on content-matched replies, not why: we did not train the released models, and the preference-data audit is correlational. Our causal re-run uses OLMo-2-1B, and its effect appears only at the largest dose we tested and varies across training runs. On OLMo-2-1B, CAP passes M1 and M4 but fails M2, M3 and M5, and on Qwen3-8B it does not pass M1 (Section B.3); the prestige contrast pairs spelling cues with grammatical and lexical dialect features, so it does not separate social prestige from feature type; it is tested with rendered requests and trained-feature targets, and it under-accommodates. We measure asymmetry, not optimal behaviour; whether and when model should reply in users variety is for its speakers to decide (Sandoval et al., 2025). items by their WildChat identifiers, without their text) and all derived results. The replies of the deployed chatbots will be released subject to the providers terms. Corpora whose licences do not state redistribution (the AAE tweets and EnDive) are not re-shared; the code release includes scripts that rebuild their twins from the original sources. We do not release the re-trained checkpoints. People. No crowdworkers or external participants were involved. All human labels are consensus labels from panel of five or more annotators with PhD-level training in related fields, agreed through discussion; an author recorded them with software tool. They cover blind audit of 84 items of model-generated text, blind sample of 20 WildChat user requests and 40 replies in the blind CAP naturalness check (Section 6). The items were not annotated independently, so no inter-annotator agreement is reported. No other human labels exist, and any LLM labels are reported as such. Framing and dual use. Accommodation is not quantity to maximize: over-accommodation can caricature and stereotype (Fleisig et al., 2024), and Black American participants want choice (Sandoval et al., 2025). Our re-run shows that large dose of accommodation-consistent preference pairs switches accommodation on, and that in one of 4 runs it over-produces the trained features, which risks caricature. AI assistance. AI assistants were used for code writing and polish but the whole research is design and checked by researchers.

GPU-hours in total); the GRPO runs used 4-GPU jobs with verl 0.9.1. B.1 Experimental Details This section gives the stimuli, prompts, framings and decoding settings. Stimuli. The 287 first-person requests span six task types (advice, creative, how-to, opinion and small talk, 50 each; explanation, 37) and carry context tag (150 formal, 137 casual). Each request is rendered in every condition with its content fixed. Morphosyntactic features are applied by Multi-VALUE (Ziems et al., 2023) with each Generic style instruction Match the users style and register. Persona You are an assistant from {community}. In the explicit request, {variety} is African American English or Colloquial Singapore English (Singlish); the persona names the varietys community (e.g. the African American community, Singapore). The style instruction and the persona are given with both the variety request and its Standard-English twin, so convergence is measured under the same instruction on both sides. Decoding. All open models are run with vLLM at temperature 0.7 and top-p 0.95, with at most 400 new tokens, three sampling seeds and 2 samples per request and seed (one sample under the explicit request). Precision exceeds .80, but its lower bound is below .60. As pre-declared, competence is therefore reported at the human-corrected rate, precision times detector rate (Section 4.2). The descriptions of these two features were drafted for the audit and used without the planned review. Restricted to the retained AAE features that the protocol specifies, the panel confirmed all 6 hits (lower bound 0.610). We chose this restriction after labelling, so it is sensitivity analysis and does not change the decision. Detector hits on default replies are noisy. The panel confirmed 6 of 14 hits: all 4 for aint and 2 for completive done, but none of the 4 for multiple negation or the 4 for completive finish. Real features are rare in these replies, so precision among hits is low even at the per-reply false-positive rates of the validity gate. The aligned-stage convergence these counts feed is near zero (Section 4.1). Fewer detectorpositive items than planned existed for can/cannot, completive finish and completive done; per-item provenance, shortages and the scoring script are in the code release (https://anonymous.4open. science/r/cap-accommodation/). LLM judges. Two open-weight LLMs from families, openai/gpt-oss-20b and different Qwen/Qwen3-8B, labelled the same 84 items blind, with the panels instructions and options, fixed prompt and greedy decoding (prompt and settings in the code release). On the 44 feature items, gptoss-20b gives the consensus label on 43 (κ = 0.95) and Qwen3-8B on 34 (κ = 0.43). On the 40 register pairs, the judges call 3 and 0 pairs equally formal, against the panels 25; where the panel picked reply, gpt-oss-20b picked the same one in 14 of 15 pairs and Qwen3-8B in 12 of 15. The two judges agree with each other on 33 feature items and 30 register pairs. The judges ran after the human labels were in, and no validation rule or reported effect uses their labels. B.3 Calibrated Accommodation Pairs This section gives the CAP setup, its pre-declared criteria, pair construction and training details. Pre-declared criteria and pair audit. Analysis code and criteria were frozen before any result (D24, in the code release). M1: held-out convergence above the control by at least 0.02 with 95% CI above zero, from bootstrap over training runs and requests. M2: per variety, reply-touser density ratio closer to 1 than the one-sided recipes, fewer replies above twice the users density, and at most 0.05 inserted features per 100 words for Standard-English users. M3: positive within-request tracking slope, above the one-sided recipes. M4: IFEval within two points, on the CI. M5: no more dialect than the control under request for Standard English. Before training, an audit found no held-out features in the pairs and length or punctuation differences of one to two words in opposite directions across pair types; only 0.39 of the mirrored replies land within 25% of the users density, 1.9 features below it on average, because many replies offer too few sentences to render, and the over-dense replies are also less fluent under the SFT model (0.18 nats per token). U, against under-accommodation: dialect request; chosen, the reply re-rendered at the users density (the subset of sentences whose achieved density is closest to the users, at most 1.25 times it); rejected, the standard reply. O, against over-accommodation: the same request; chosen as in U; rejected, every sentence re-rendered, kept only with at least twice the chosen replys features. A, against imposition: the Standard-English twin; chosen, the standard reply; rejected, every sentence re-rendered. The mix is : : = 2 : 1 : 1 over AAE and Singlish, at third of the DPO pairs (Figure 6, Section 6). Candidates carry only the trained features, so held-out features and varieties test transfer. OLMo-2-1B. The released recipe on the 120k subset of its preference mix plus 60k CAP pairs, three training runs, compared with the matched controls and one-sided pairs of Section 5.2; an ablation replaces the pairs by pairs, and further baseline fine-tunes on the re-rendered replies before DPO; two runs drop the pairs, and two runs build the one-sided recipe with CAPs pair builder (predeclared confound control, filed before its result: the registered one-sided pairs predate formatting fix). Qwen3-8B. As pre-registered (D24, in the code release), we also trained CAP on Qwen3-8B (LoRA-DPO, three runs per arm); it did not pass M1, raising held-out convergence by 0.017 (CI [0.009, 0.026]) against the 0.02 minimum. In blind check of 40 of its replies, the expert panels consensus labels mark 0 of 20 CAP replies and 0 of 20 one-sided replies exaggerated, so the check does not separate them. Evaluation. 300 fresh requests from disjoint pool, rendered as in Section 3: held-out-feature and held-out-variety convergence; the ratio of reply to user density and the share of replies above twice the users; dialect features in replies to StandardEnglish users; density intervention that renders each request at two densities; compliance with explicit requests for Standard English or for variety; IFEval and GSM8K. B.4 Further Method Details Details of the requests, lineages, measures and measurement checks summarized in Sections 1 and 3. Rarity in traffic and training data. After human check of our recognisers hits, about 0.12% of 162,842 English first turns in WildChat (Zhao et al., 2024) carry an audited AAE feature (95% CI 0.040.25%), and the recognisers fire on only 0.65% of the prompts in an open preference mix (Section C.2). Lineages. OLMo-2 at four sizes, OLMo-3-7B, OLMo-3.1-32B, Tülu-3, Tülu-2 at two sizes and Zephyr (Team OLMo et al., 2025; Team Olmo, 2025; Lambert et al., 2024; Ivison et al., 2023; Tunstall et al., 2023), starting from the base model in 7 of them; each checkpoint answers 287 requests, each written in 6 varieties and in Standard English. and data artefacts. Code Released are https://anonymous.4open.science/r/ at cap-accommodation/, including 287 requests rendered in 6 varieties, two registers and Standard English with their validity gates and feature detectors checked against blind audit of 84 items and WildChat precision check of 20 items, both labelled by consensus of panel of five or more annotators with PhD-level training in related fields; the replies of 5 deployed chatbots follow on publication. Prestige tiers and renderings. The varieties are ordered by prestige tiers that we pre-registered from attitude studies (Coupland and Bishop, 2007; Bernaisch and Koch, 2016; Cavallaro et al., 2014; Purnell et al., 1999; Rickford and King, 2016; Luhman, 1990; Obi, 2014). Morphosyntax follows the eWAVE rules of Multi-VALUE (Ziems et al., 2023), applied at the eWAVE attestation rates scaled by 0.8; lexis, particles and spelling follow curated lexicons (Section B.1). Lineages and sampling. We study lineages whose every post-training stage is public, so consecutive checkpoints differ by one training stage: OLMo-2 at 1B, 7B, 13B and 32B (Team OLMo et al., 2025) and OLMo-3-7B (Team Olmo, 2025), each with base, SFT, DPO and RLVR checkpoints, Tülu-3-8Bs SFT, DPO and RLVR stages (Lambert et al., 2024) and Tülu-2s SFT and DPO stages at 7B and 13B (Ivison et al., 2023), whose bases are gated, Zephyr-7B-βs base, SFT and DPO stages (Tunstall et al., 2023), and OLMo-3.1-32Bs base, SFT, DPO and RLVR stages (Team Olmo, 2025). Qwen2.5-72B tests scale, and widely used families and deployed chatbots test breadth, at their released stages (Section A.1). Aligned stages use their own chat template; base stages are run as raw continuation, under the chat template, and in transcript scaffold (Section B.1). We sample 2 replies per request for each of 3 sampling seeds, at temperature 0.7 and top-p 0.95. Uncounted features. Some salient features fail our false-positive check on standard text and are not counted; the sister examples keep (no third-person -s) is one, while its yall is counted (Section B.2). Validity checks. Two pre-registered validity checks decide how each cue is read: every counted variety feature must fire on at most 2% of replies to SAE requests at every stage  (Table 9)  , and at least 60% of replies must offer three or more opportunities. Spelling and the lexis-carried varieties (SGE, NGP) fail the second check at some or all stages, so for them we use the rate-based ratio, with realizations per 100 words in place of densities; for AAE the two ratios agree. Reading the ratio. CRv = 1 means that the replies differ between the variety and its StandardEnglish twin by as much as the requests do, 0 that they do not differ, and negative values reversed difference; the ratio does not measure absolute matching to the users density. Implicit reward. For the length-normalized DPO recipe of OLMo 2 and Tülu 3, βˆrm is the score inside the training loss, so its differences between replies to the same request are implicitreward differences; for the other recipes we read it as descriptive update score. The matched and standard replies differ only in the rendered variety features, including some that the convergence ratio does not count (keeps versus keep). Compute. At least 298 GPU hours on NVIDIA H800s, 185 of them for the DPO re-runs; API queries to deployed chatbots are logged with their cost in the released repository. Measurement validity. An expert panel assigned consensus labels to 84 blind items (Table 10 in Section B.2). On requested replies, the consensus labels and detectors agree on 28 of 30 items (κ = 0.814), and the panel confirmed 6 of 7 detector hits. The GYAFC-trained formality ranker that the protocol named, run after labelling, picks the panels more formal reply in 12 of 15 pairs; the part-of-speech score does not pass (9 of 15), and no claim rests on it. On raw user requests the recognisers over-fire: of 18 WildChat requests they flagged, the expert panel confirmed 3. We therefore apply them only to model replies. Default replies carry few hits, and the panel confirmed 6 of 14; the false ones, mostly multiple negation (confirmed in 0 of 4), occur about as often in replies to the StandardEnglish twins (146 against 121 hits over 30,996 replies each after post-training), so they largely cancel in the ratio, and default convergence remains subject to this detector error (Section B.2). Prior function-word measures barely move between varieties and stages, and instructions, personas and copying do not explain the pattern (Section C.1). B.5 Further CAP Details Settings, pilot, registered criteria, ablations and sensitivity of Section 6 in full. What the pairs express. CAPs pairs express preferences against sampled underand overaccommodation; we do not claim reward that peaks at the users density. The three pair types the matching and anchoring do different work: contrasts carry the gain, the over-accommodation contrast buys restraint, and density matching curbs the Singlish overshoot (Section 6.3). Settings. We train OLMo-2-1B, whose stages are all released and whose controls from Section 5.2 carry over, with fixed budget in every arm (Table 11 in Section B.3). Arms share prompts and pair counts. The test set is 300 fresh requests from pool disjoint from training, validation and the requests of Section 4. We compare CAP with control that prefers one standard reply over another and with the one-sided pairs of Section 5.2, at the same budget, and, without training, with the unchanged model  (Table 11)  . Pilot. The pre-declared pilot on OLMo-2-1B passed 3 of 4 checks on validation requests. Its trained-feature convergence exceeds the control by 0.38 (CI [0.35, 0.41]), and it inserts no dialect into replies to Standard-English users (0.002 features per 100 words against the control). Its calibration falls below the pre-declared band: CAP underaccommodates, reproducing 0.50 of the users density for AAE and 0.26 for Singlish, as the audit of its pairs anticipated (Section B.3). We continue as pre-declared, without tuning on the pilot. Registered criteria M2, M3 and M5. Its AAE replies stay as far below the users density as the one-sided pairs (0.17 against 0.18 of it), and its Singlish replies no longer overshoot (0.79 against 2.59); the Singlish difference is not resolved, because the one-sided runs vary widely, so M2 fails as registered. The one-sided pairs track the users Singlish density more steeply, by overshooting it (slope 3.606 against 0.191; M3 fails), and neither recipe makes the 1B model follow request for Standard English (0.680 and 0.954 more features per 100 words than the control; M5 fails). Ablation variants. Each ablation removes one component of CAP on OLMo-2-1B at the same budget: the pairs (their slots filled with pairs), the pairs, the preference contrast itself (SFT on the mirrored replies, then DPO on control pairs), and density matching (the one-sided pairs of Section 5.2, and, as pre-declared control for their older pair builder, the same recipe built with CAPs builder); an exploratory run raises the mirror target to 1.5 times the users density. Ablation results. Table 5 isolates the pairs. Without them, held-out convergence rises to 0.583 over the control (2 runs), but the model imposes dialect: replies to Standard-English users gain 0.039 features per 100 words, and replies to request for Standard English keep 7.36. The pairs thus trade convergence for restraint, the behaviour CAP is built to keep; the registered one-sided pairs gain less (0.043) and insert more (0.560). Imitation is not enough: fine-tuning on the same mirrored replies before DPO leaves held-out convergence unchanged (0.001) and costs 5.9 IFEval points, so the gain comes from the preference contrast. Within CAPs mix, the pairs matter as much: without them, held-out convergence barely moves (0.008, 2 runs). The mirror target sets how far CAP accommodates: raising it to 1.5 times the users density, in an exploratory run, multiplies held-out convergence by 2.0 (0.340) without insertion (0.007). Density matching is what curbs the overshoot, although AAE replies remain well below the users density. Built with CAPs builder, the one-sided pairs raise held-out convergence by 0.201 (CI [0.139, 0.269], 2 runs), gain similar to CAPs, but by overshooting: their Singlish replies reach 10.41 times the users density, 95% of them above twice it (CAP: 0.79, 0%), replies to StandardEnglish users gain 0.378 features per 100 words, and replies to request for Standard English keep 2.42. Sensitivity of the CAP gain. CAPs held-out gain on OLMo-2-1B does not depend on how it is estimated or where it is tested. bootstrap over requests alone narrows its interval to [0.151, 0.198] (registered, over runs and requests: [0.138, 0.207]); dropping the 2% false-positive exclusion leaves it at 0.173; and on the 287 requests of Section 4, used before the method existed, it is 0.137 (CI [0.108, 0.167]).

An audit that inspects replies finds the same Standard-English answer for every user and cannot tell whether training treats varieties alike. The update diagnostic shows that it does not: it moves the policy toward matching some users and away from matching others. This preference does not show in the default output, and content-matched reply pairs read it from public checkpoints without retraining. We recommend that model releases report it next to output audits when consecutive checkpoints are public. The standard default arises with little dialectspecific data. Convergence falls at the preference stage on data in which fewer than 1% of prompts carry detectable dialect feature, and the ability to produce AAE features on request survives. The default is thus consistent with the form that general post-training data favour, in line with the mostly stylistic shifts that alignment tuning produces (Lin et al., 2024a). Deployed chatbots that answer Nigerian Pidgin in kind (Section 4.1) show that standardizing stigmatized variety is not inevitable after post-training. Accommodation-consistent preference pairs raise convergence, though without calibration to the user (Section 5.2), and some capacity to produce the features remains accessible on request. Prestige differences persist in the update. CAT predicts convergence toward prestige. After alignment, the replies of our models show little convergence of any kind, but after adjustment the updates of all 10 lineages still favour matching prestige spelling over stigmatized varieties, and the ordering of behaviour by prestige is already present at the base checkpoints. The ordering is consistent with prestige-directed convergence but does not identify prestige as its cause. Raw and adjusted contrasts answer different questions: OLMo-2-32Bs update up-weights unlikely replies in general, so its contrast is 0.031 on the observed pairs and 0.012 after adjustment, and diagnostics of an update should report both. Aligned chat models are thus interlocutors whose surface behaviour is uniform while their learned preferences are not. The two accounts therefore make different predictions for language models: priming predicts convergence to every variety, while CAT predicts convergence that depends on the social value of the variety. We use CAT only as source of such predictions; we make no claim about model intentions. Standard-language ideology supplies the ordering. Standard-language ideology holds that one variety is correct and that the others are errors (Milroy, 2001; Milroy and Milroy, 2012). Institutions reproduce it by rewarding the standard (LippiGreen, 2012). Its stigma falls on racialized and postcolonial speakers even when they use standard forms (Rosa and Flores, 2017), and matched-guise experiments measure it as covert evaluation from speech alone (Lambert et al., 1960; Hofmann et al., 2024). Smith et al. (2026) argue that generative AI reproduces this ideology; we measure it. Under the ideology, upward convergence has predictable shape. Models should converge to the standard and to prestige cues, including an informal but standard register. They should maintain or diverge from stigmatized morphosyntax, which the ideology classes as wrong grammar. And they should keep the competence to produce it. Is the standard-English default of chat models learned by imitating standard responses, or installed by preferring them? CAT separates what speaker produces from what the speaker is disposed to do. There are 287 requests instead of 300. The human audit was scored against the formality score actually used, and it included two Singlish features outside its specification (Section B.2). The LLM reference-label pass was dropped. The paired test of the update diagnostic was added. 60k dose was added to the DPO re-runs (Section D.2). The bootstrap resamples requests without the preregistered stratification by task type. Resampling within task type leaves all 10 adjusted contrasts of Section 5 above zero, with intervals 0.931.02 times as wide.

sections.title: E Related Work
sections.content: Prior work on accommodation in language models, dialect bias and post-training. E.1 Related Work This section reviews prior work on accommodation in language models, dialect bias and post-training. Accommodation in language models. Accommodation is measured as style matching in word use (Niederhoffer and Pennebaker, 2002; Ireland and Pennebaker, 2010), as the coordination of style markers (Danescu-Niculescu-Mizil et al., 2011, 2012), or as baseline-corrected lexical and syntactic alignment (Nenkova et al., 2008; Doyle et al., 2016; Duran et al., 2019); these measures are sensitive to low-level confounds such as utterance length (Xu et al., 2018; Litterer et al., 2025). Language models converge strongly when completing human dialogues, and instruction-tuned models converge less (Blevins et al., 2026); deployed chat models overconverge to their users style in the wild (Blevins, 2026), although convergence in humanChatGPT dialogue declines over turns (Mitiaeva and Xiao, 2026). LLM replies match their partners style less than humans do (Durandard et al., 2025a,b) and entrain less than therapists (Kian et al., 2025); alignment also depends on the interlocutor, falling below human levels with children though not with adults (French et al., 2024) and better for higher socioeconomic groups (Bassignana et al., 2026). Models also favour tokens seen in the context, even irrelevant ones (Niu et al., 2025; Kukreja et al., 2026), which convergence measure must discount as copying. Unlike these works, which measure style, we measure the features that distinguish varietiesspelling, register and dialect grammarat every released post-training stage, and we separate what the model does from what its update favours. Homogenization or directed standardization? Post-training is associated with reduced output diversity (Kirk et al., 2024; Padmakumar and He, 2024; West and Potts, 2025; Gude et al., 2026), which has been traced to typicality bias in preference data (Zhang et al., 2025a) and located in particular post-training stages (Karouzos et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026). On the superficial-alignment view, models learn the format of replies from little finetuning data (Zhou et al., 2023), and alignment tuning shifts mostly stylistic tokens (Lin et al., 2024a). Direction matters as much as variance: AI writing suggestions pull Indian writers toward Western styles (Agarwal et al., 2025), LLM rewriting erases South Asian English markers (Bharati et al., 2026), and chat models answer speakers of other varieties in standard variety (Fleisig et al., 2024). Homogenization predicts that replies vary less; we test directed shift instead, in which replies to every informal cue move toward one standard at both finetuning stages, in line with the superficial-alignment view, while the update is not variety-neutral. Reward models, preference data and dialect. Reward models disprefer African American Language and steer conversations toward White Mainstream English (Mire et al., 2025); across the pipeline, dialect gaps accumulate and rewardmodel preferences between dialect versions of problem change sign across tasks (Elle, 2026); preference tuning creates disparities between English dialects (Ryan et al., 2024); and reward models are weaker outside English (Gureja et al., 2025). Preference models also reward surface form: length (Singhal et al., 2024), lists, bold text and emojis (Zhang et al., 2025b), and human and LLM judges rate fluent answers above factually correct ones (Wu and Aji, 2025); preference-tuned models also defer to users views (Sharma et al., 2024). Unlike these studies, which score fixed texts with reward model or judge, we read the policys own update on content-matched replies that differ only in whether they match the users variety. Likelihood-ratio diagnostics of post-training. Direct preference optimization makes the log-ratio between policy and reference an implicit reward (Rafailov et al., 2023), interpretable at the token level (Rafailov et al., 2024), and reward benchmarks evaluate it alongside explicit reward models (Lambert et al., 2025). As reward model it generalizes less well than an explicit one (Lin et al., 2024b), and preference-tuned models often fail to rank preferred responses above rejected ones (Chen et al., 2024). Differences between tuned and an untuned models log-probabilities also isolate what fine-tuning adds and can transfer it across scales (Mitchell et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024). We use the ratio descriptively, as an update diagnostic: comparing it across content-matched replies shows which reply forms training stage upor down-weights given the users variety. We do not treat it as an identified reward, and we read the SFT-versus-base ratio as likelihood shift only. Standards, ideology and who is affected. Standard-language ideology treats one variety as correct and others as errors (Milroy, 2001; LippiGreen, 2012); sociolinguistics distinguishes monocentric from pluricentric languages, whose national varieties have their own norms (Clyne, 1992), and postcolonial Englishes can develop endonormative standards (Schneider, 2003). Recent work argues that generative AI reproduces this ideology (Smith et al., 2026; Ugwuanyi, 2026). The fairness literature documents its costs: covert dialect prejudice revealed by matched-guise probing (Hofmann et al., 2024) and by paired dialectstandard comparisons (Bui et al., 2025), which human-feedback alignment conceals rather than removes (Hofmann et al., 2024) and side-by-side comparison amplifies (Kondapally et al., 2026); dialect-dependent safety behaviour (Haq and Saldaías, 2026); harms that must be named against normative standard (Blodgett et al., 2020); and adaptation labour shifted onto speakers (Cunningham et al., 2024). Speakers want control over when variety is used: Black American participants prefer Mainstream U.S. English in formal settings and are more open to AAE in informal ones (Sandoval et al., 2025), and preferences differ between text and spoken AAE chatbots (Finch et al., 2025). Our results are consistent with, but do not by themselves establish, monocentric standard in post-training. They give sociolinguists test of accommodation theory with machine interlocutors, alignment researchers diagnostic of what preference data teach beyond content, and auditors way to separate what model does from what its training favours.
